changes._why: the RANK form kept the employee with no department as a partition, unlike the correlated form; DESC put a NULL salary first; no tie order
request: Each department head is told who their best-paid employee is; ties are all reported, ordered by `EMPLOYEE_ID`.
An employee with no department is left out, as the correlated solution leaves them out; `NULLS LAST` keeps a salary not recorded from ranking first, which Oracle's `DESC` would do.
changes.sql:
SELECT DEPARTMENT_ID, EMPLOYEE_ID, LAST_NAME, SALARY
FROM (SELECT e.*, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY DEPARTMENT_ID ORDER BY SALARY DESC NULLS LAST) AS RNK
      FROM EMPLOYEES e
      WHERE DEPARTMENT_ID IS NOT NULL)
WHERE RNK = 1
ORDER BY DEPARTMENT_ID ASC, EMPLOYEE_ID ASC

changes._why: DESC put a NULL salary first, at DENSE_RANK 1; three salaries, not three people; no tie order
request: Ahead of the bonus round, each department head wants the three highest salaries of the department and everyone who earns one of them, ties included.
`NULLS LAST` keeps a salary not recorded from ranking first; the people of one rank are ordered by `EMPLOYEE_ID`.
changes.sql:
SELECT DEPARTMENT_ID, EMPLOYEE_ID, LAST_NAME, SALARY, RNK
FROM (SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY DEPARTMENT_ID ORDER BY SALARY DESC NULLS LAST) AS RNK
      FROM EMPLOYEES e
      WHERE DEPARTMENT_ID IS NOT NULL)
WHERE RNK <= 3
ORDER BY DEPARTMENT_ID ASC, RNK ASC, EMPLOYEE_ID ASC

changes._why: the view passes SALARY through as nullable, and DESC put a NULL first; LAST_NAME does not break a tie of two people of one name
request: Each regional director is told who the best-paid people in their region are: the three highest salaries, ties included, ordered by last name and `EMPLOYEE_ID`.
`NULLS LAST` keeps a salary not recorded from ranking first.
changes.sql:
SELECT REGION_NAME, EMPLOYEE_ID, LAST_NAME, JOB_TITLE, SALARY, RNK
FROM (SELECT v.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY REGION_NAME ORDER BY SALARY DESC NULLS LAST) AS RNK
      FROM EMP_DETAILS_VIEW v)
WHERE RNK <= 3
ORDER BY REGION_NAME ASC, RNK ASC, LAST_NAME ASC, EMPLOYEE_ID ASC

changes._why: HIRE_DATE is a DATE, which has a time; BETWEEN missed a hire later on the last day, which the note admitted; no tie order
request: HR is preparing the probation review for everyone hired in a given period, the from and to dates both included, the earliest hires first; people hired on one day are ordered by `EMPLOYEE_ID`.
A `DATE` has a time of day, so the period runs from `TRUNC(:fromDate)` up to, not including, the day after `:toDate`.
changes.sql:
SELECT *
FROM EMPLOYEES
WHERE HIRE_DATE >= TRUNC(:fromDate)
  AND HIRE_DATE < TRUNC(:toDate) + 1
ORDER BY HIRE_DATE ASC, EMPLOYEE_ID ASC

changes._why: the update_job_history trigger writes END_DATE as SYSDATE, with a time; BETWEEN missed a position closed later on the last day
request: For an audit, HR wants every earlier position that ended within a given period, the from and to dates both included, the earliest endings first.
The schema's trigger writes `END_DATE` as `SYSDATE`, which has a time of day, so the period runs up to, not including, the day after `:toDate`.
changes.sql:
SELECT EMPLOYEE_ID, START_DATE, END_DATE, JOB_ID, DEPARTMENT_ID
FROM JOB_HISTORY
WHERE END_DATE >= TRUNC(:fromDate)
  AND END_DATE < TRUNC(:toDate) + 1
ORDER BY END_DATE ASC, EMPLOYEE_ID ASC, START_DATE ASC

changes._why: END_DATE from SYSDATE has a time, so END_DATE - START_DATE + 1 became a fraction of a day; TRUNC gives whole days
request: Workforce planning wants to know how long people stay in a job before they move on: per job, the number of earlier positions and the shortest, average and longest of them in whole days, the longest average first.
`TRUNC` takes each date to its day, since the trigger writes `END_DATE` with a time.
changes.sql:
SELECT JOB_ID,
       COUNT(*)                                            AS POSITIONS,
       MIN(TRUNC(END_DATE) - TRUNC(START_DATE) + 1)        AS SHORTEST_DAYS,
       ROUND(AVG(TRUNC(END_DATE) - TRUNC(START_DATE) + 1)) AS AVERAGE_DAYS,
       MAX(TRUNC(END_DATE) - TRUNC(START_DATE) + 1)        AS LONGEST_DAYS
FROM JOB_HISTORY
GROUP BY JOB_ID
ORDER BY AVERAGE_DAYS DESC, JOB_ID ASC

changes._why: ELSE counted a salary not recorded as High, as SAKILA_FILM_I_03 counted a NULL length as long; no ORDER BY
request: HR reports headcount in three pay grades: under 5,000, 5,000 up to 10,000, and 10,000 or more, with the employees whose salary is not recorded in a fourth, `Not recorded`.
Show the grades from the lowest to the highest, `Not recorded` last.
changes.sql:
SELECT CASE
           WHEN SALARY IS NULL THEN 'Not recorded'
           WHEN SALARY < 5000 THEN 'Low'
           WHEN SALARY < 10000 THEN 'Medium'
           ELSE 'High'
           END  AS GRADE,
       COUNT(*) AS HEADCOUNT
FROM EMPLOYEES
GROUP BY CASE
             WHEN SALARY IS NULL THEN 'Not recorded'
             WHEN SALARY < 5000 THEN 'Low'
             WHEN SALARY < 10000 THEN 'Medium'
             ELSE 'High'
             END
ORDER BY MIN(SALARY) ASC NULLS LAST

changes._why: HIRE_DATE was shown as the start of the current job (Codex), and the current job could sort before an earlier one of the same date (Claude); the current job starts the day after the last END_DATE, or on HIRE_DATE with no history
request: An employee asks HR for their record: every position they have held, the current one included, in date order.

The trigger writes an earlier position's end when the job changes, so the current position starts the day after the last `END_DATE` of the history, or on `HIRE_DATE` if there is none; the current one, with no end, comes last on a tie.
changes.sql:
SELECT h.START_DATE, h.END_DATE, h.JOB_ID, j.JOB_TITLE, h.DEPARTMENT_ID
FROM JOB_HISTORY h
         JOIN JOBS j ON j.JOB_ID = h.JOB_ID
WHERE h.EMPLOYEE_ID = :employeeId
UNION ALL
SELECT COALESCE((SELECT TRUNC(MAX(h2.END_DATE)) + 1 FROM JOB_HISTORY h2 WHERE h2.EMPLOYEE_ID = e.EMPLOYEE_ID), e.HIRE_DATE),
       NULL,
       e.JOB_ID,
       j.JOB_TITLE,
       e.DEPARTMENT_ID
FROM EMPLOYEES e
         JOIN JOBS j ON j.JOB_ID = e.JOB_ID
WHERE e.EMPLOYEE_ID = :employeeId
ORDER BY 1 ASC, 2 ASC NULLS LAST

changes._why: d.*, e.* gave DEPARTMENT_ID and MANAGER_ID twice under one name (Claude); people of one surname were in no order (Codex)
request: The intranet's site page shows, for one location, each department and its staff, the empty departments included, the staff by last name, first name and `EMPLOYEE_ID`.
Loading the departments and then each one's employees is the N+1 problem; the page needs a single query, with each column named once.
changes.sql:
SELECT d.DEPARTMENT_ID, d.DEPARTMENT_NAME, e.EMPLOYEE_ID, e.FIRST_NAME, e.LAST_NAME, e.JOB_ID
FROM DEPARTMENTS d
         LEFT JOIN EMPLOYEES e ON e.DEPARTMENT_ID = d.DEPARTMENT_ID
WHERE d.LOCATION_ID = :locationId
ORDER BY d.DEPARTMENT_ID ASC, e.LAST_NAME ASC, e.FIRST_NAME ASC NULLS FIRST, e.EMPLOYEE_ID ASC

changes._why: salaries repeat, so SALARY DESC alone left an unstable order
request: The board asks who earns more than the company-wide average salary, the highest first; people with the same salary are ordered by `EMPLOYEE_ID`.
changes.sql:
SELECT EMPLOYEE_ID, FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME, SALARY
FROM EMPLOYEES
WHERE SALARY > (SELECT AVG(SALARY) FROM EMPLOYEES)
ORDER BY SALARY DESC, EMPLOYEE_ID ASC

changes._why: no ORDER BY; MINUS sorts on many plans, but nothing promises it
request: Facilities is reviewing the property list: which locations host no department at all, by `LOCATION_ID`?
`MINUS` takes away the rows of the second query; it promises no order, so the query states one.
changes.sql:
SELECT LOCATION_ID
FROM LOCATIONS
MINUS
SELECT LOCATION_ID
FROM DEPARTMENTS
ORDER BY 1 ASC

changes._why: the inner join left out an empty department, which a threshold of 0 asks for; no tie order
request: List the departments with at least `:minHeadcount` employees, a number of `0` or more, the largest first; departments of one size are ordered by `DEPARTMENT_ID`.
An outer join keeps an empty department, which a threshold of `0` includes.
changes.sql:
SELECT d.DEPARTMENT_ID, d.DEPARTMENT_NAME, COUNT(e.EMPLOYEE_ID) AS HEADCOUNT
FROM DEPARTMENTS d
         LEFT JOIN EMPLOYEES e ON e.DEPARTMENT_ID = d.DEPARTMENT_ID
GROUP BY d.DEPARTMENT_ID, d.DEPARTMENT_NAME
HAVING COUNT(e.EMPLOYEE_ID) >= :minHeadcount
ORDER BY HEADCOUNT DESC, d.DEPARTMENT_ID ASC

changes._why: 'the top tenth of the band' and '90% of the maximum' are two thresholds; the stated one kept, the order by the unrounded share
request: HR lists the employees paid at least 90% of their job's maximum salary, as due for a promotion conversation, the highest share first; `EMPLOYEE_ID` breaks a tie.
changes.sql:
SELECT e.EMPLOYEE_ID, e.FIRST_NAME, e.LAST_NAME, e.JOB_ID, e.SALARY, j.MAX_SALARY
FROM EMPLOYEES e
         JOIN JOBS j ON j.JOB_ID = e.JOB_ID
WHERE e.SALARY >= j.MAX_SALARY * 0.9
ORDER BY e.SALARY / NULLIF(j.MAX_SALARY, 0) DESC NULLS LAST, e.EMPLOYEE_ID ASC

changes._why: CHECK (salary > 0) lets a salary be NULL; the rankings assume every employee has one
changes.title: Salaries not recorded
request: `CHECK (salary > 0)` lets a salary be NULL, while the exercises that rank salaries assume every employee has one.
Payroll wants the employees whose salary is not recorded, by `EMPLOYEE_ID`; the check passes when nothing comes back.
changes.sql:
SELECT EMPLOYEE_ID, FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME, JOB_ID
FROM EMPLOYEES
WHERE SALARY IS NULL
ORDER BY EMPLOYEE_ID ASC

changes._why: no exercise takes only the top n rows, Oracle's FETCH FIRST (setMaxResults in JPQL)
changes.title: The newest hires
request: The onboarding team wants the `:n` most recently hired employees, the newest first; people hired on one day are ordered by `EMPLOYEE_ID`, the highest first.
`FETCH FIRST :n ROWS ONLY` takes the first rows, with no offset for the first page.
changes.sql:
SELECT EMPLOYEE_ID, FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME, JOB_ID, HIRE_DATE
FROM EMPLOYEES
ORDER BY HIRE_DATE DESC, EMPLOYEE_ID DESC
FETCH FIRST :n ROWS ONLY

changes._why: nothing makes a salary band complete, positive or in order, which the ratio and career exercises assume
changes.title: Salary bands needing repair
request: Nothing in the schema makes a job's salary band complete, positive, or its minimum below its maximum, which the exercises on bands assume.
Find the jobs with a bound missing, a bound not above `0`, or a minimum above the maximum, by `JOB_ID`; the check passes when nothing comes back.
changes.sql:
SELECT JOB_ID, JOB_TITLE, MIN_SALARY, MAX_SALARY
FROM JOBS
WHERE MIN_SALARY IS NULL
   OR MAX_SALARY IS NULL
   OR MIN_SALARY <= 0
   OR MAX_SALARY <= 0
   OR MIN_SALARY > MAX_SALARY
ORDER BY JOB_ID ASC

changes._why: DEPARTMENTS.MANAGER_ID and the manager's own DEPARTMENT_ID are two independent links, and nothing ties them
changes.title: Managers outside their department
request: An auditor wants every department whose manager on record is not a member of that department, or of none, with the department the manager does belong to.
changes.sql:
SELECT d.DEPARTMENT_ID, d.DEPARTMENT_NAME, m.EMPLOYEE_ID, m.LAST_NAME, m.DEPARTMENT_ID AS MANAGER_DEPARTMENT_ID
FROM DEPARTMENTS d
         JOIN EMPLOYEES m ON m.EMPLOYEE_ID = d.MANAGER_ID
WHERE m.DEPARTMENT_ID IS NULL
   OR m.DEPARTMENT_ID <> d.DEPARTMENT_ID
ORDER BY d.DEPARTMENT_ID ASC

changes._why: the country and location counts leave out a country with no site; the anti-join from countries to locations
changes.title: Countries without a company site
request: Which countries of the catalogue have no company site, by name?
changes.sql:
SELECT c.COUNTRY_ID, c.COUNTRY_NAME
FROM COUNTRIES c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM LOCATIONS l WHERE l.COUNTRY_ID = c.COUNTRY_ID)
ORDER BY c.COUNTRY_NAME ASC, c.COUNTRY_ID ASC

changes._why: string aggregation, LISTAGG ... WITHIN GROUP, is missing from the set
changes.title: Each department's staff on one line
request: The intranet's department index shows each department with its headcount and its staff's last names on one line, alphabetically.
`LISTAGG ... WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...)` joins the names in order.
changes.sql:
SELECT d.DEPARTMENT_ID,
       d.DEPARTMENT_NAME,
       COUNT(*)                                                                          AS HEADCOUNT,
       LISTAGG(e.LAST_NAME, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY e.LAST_NAME, e.EMPLOYEE_ID) AS STAFF
FROM DEPARTMENTS d
         JOIN EMPLOYEES e ON e.DEPARTMENT_ID = d.DEPARTMENT_ID
GROUP BY d.DEPARTMENT_ID, d.DEPARTMENT_NAME
ORDER BY d.DEPARTMENT_ID ASC

changes._why: the per-country payroll has no subtotals, and GROUP BY ROLLUP and GROUPING appear nowhere
changes.title: Payroll with subtotals
request: Finance wants the monthly salary cost per country, with a subtotal for each region and a grand total.
`GROUP BY ROLLUP` adds the subtotal rows, and `GROUPING` tells them from the others.
changes.sql:
SELECT REGION_NAME,
       COUNTRY_NAME,
       COUNT(*)                               AS HEADCOUNT,
       SUM(SALARY)                            AS MONTHLY_COST,
       GROUPING_ID(REGION_NAME, COUNTRY_NAME) AS SUBTOTAL_LEVEL
FROM EMP_DETAILS_VIEW
GROUP BY ROLLUP (REGION_NAME, COUNTRY_NAME)
ORDER BY GROUPING(REGION_NAME) ASC, REGION_NAME ASC, GROUPING(COUNTRY_NAME) ASC, COUNTRY_NAME ASC
